title: Explain time complexity and space complexity, with common Big-O examples.
shortTitle: Time complexity and space complexity, with common Big-O examples
keyPoints: Time complexity describes how running time scales with input size; space complexity describes how extra memory scales.
Big-O captures the dominant growth rate, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.
O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) sort, O(n squared) quadratic, O(2^n) exponential.
HashMap lookup is O(1), TreeMap lookup is O(log n), scanning a list is O(n), sorting is O(n log n), nested loop is O(n squared).
Time-space trade-off: caching balances in a map trades O(n) memory for O(1) lookup speed.
Big-O hides constants; amortized complexity matters for ArrayList; always measure on real data for the final word.

s1_definition.oneliner: Time complexity is how running time scales with input size, space complexity is how extra memory scales, and Big-O names the growth rate ignoring constants.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Time complexity** – describes how the running time of an algorithm grows as the input size grows.
- **Space complexity** – describes how the amount of extra memory grows with input size.
- **Big-O notation** – captures the dominant growth rate while ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
- **Upper bound** – Big-O gives an upper bound on growth, letting you compare algorithms independently of hardware.
- **Practical use** – predict how a solution behaves when data goes from a thousand rows to ten million.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a ledger and Rajesh wants to find an account. If the ledger is an unsorted list and he flips through every card one by one, a million customers means up to a million flips: linear time. If the cards are sorted and he uses the phone-book trick of opening the middle and halving each time, a million customers take only about twenty checks: logarithmic time. Big-O is just a way of saying "as the bank grows to millions of customers, how much slower does this method get?"

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Big-O Growth Rates (slow to fast growth)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────

  O(1)       ─────────────────────── constant
  O(log n)   ───────────/            logarithmic
  O(n)       ─────────/              linear
  O(n log n) ────────/               linearithmic
  O(n^2)     ──────/                 quadratic
  O(2^n)     ────/                   exponential

  Banking Examples:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ O(1)       HashMap.get(accountId)         │
  │ O(log n)   TreeMap.get(balance)            │
  │ O(n)       sum all transactions            │
  │ O(n log n) sort daily transactions         │
  │ O(n^2)     naive duplicate detection       │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Time-Space Trade-off:
  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │ Compute  │    │  Cache   │
  │ O(n)     │ vs │  O(1)    │ lookup
  │ O(1)     │    │  O(n)    │ memory
  │ space    │    │  space   │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Time complexity describes how an algorithm's running time grows as the input grows, and space complexity describes how its extra memory grows. Both are expressed in Big-O notation, which captures the dominant growth rate and ignores constant factors and lower-order terms, so Rajesh can compare algorithms independently of hardware and predict behaviour as data scales.

The common classes Rajesh rattles off with banking examples are these. Constant time O(1) is a `HashMap` lookup of an account by id, regardless of how many customers exist. Logarithmic O(log n) is a `TreeMap` lookup, growing by only one step each time the data doubles. Linear O(n) is summing every transaction once. O(n log n) is sorting the day's transactions. Quadratic O(n squared) is a naive double loop comparing every transaction with every other.

At National Bank of India, the fraud duplicate-check was written as a nested double loop, which is O(n squared). It ran fine on a fifty-row test file but took minutes on the real hundred-thousand-row file, because a hundred thousand squared is ten billion comparisons. Rajesh rewrote it as a single pass using a `HashSet`, which is O(n) time with O(n) extra memory, and it finished in a fraction of a second.

Space complexity follows the same logic but counts memory. The important idea is the time-space trade-off: caching precomputed balances in a map spends O(n) extra memory to turn repeated O(n) recomputation into O(1) lookups. Big-O hides constant factors and cache effects, and some operations like `ArrayList.add` are amortized O(1), so Big-O is the primary tool for reasoning about scale, but Rajesh still measures on real data for the final word.

Remember one sentence: Big-O names the growth rate ignoring constants, and the fastest win in banking is replacing an O(n squared) nested loop with an O(n) HashSet pass.
